chapter_name: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
learning_objective: 🌾 Dive deep into rural Mughal India—understand how agriculture functioned, the powerful role of Zamindars, and how the empire counted its wealth!

key_vocabulary.hindi_meaning: जमा (अनुमानित कर) और हासिल (वसूला गया कर)

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Written by Abu'l Fazl, this massive document is our main source of information about Mughal agrarian society. It details crops, yields, wages, and revenues, though it presents a top-down, idealized view from the Emperor's court.

Peasants were divided into 'Khud-kasht' (those who owned the land and lived in the village) and 'Pahi-kasht' (those who cultivated land in other villages on a contractual basis, often migrating due to famine or better terms).

While basic crops like rice, wheat, and millets were staples, the 17th century saw the arrival of new crops from the New World (via the Portuguese), most notably maize, tobacco, tomatoes, potatoes, and chilies.

Zamindars did not directly participate in agriculture but enjoyed huge social and economic privileges. They held extensive personal lands (milkiyat), collected revenue on behalf of the state, and maintained small personal armies and forts.

Land revenue was the economic backbone of the Mughal Empire. It had two stages: 'Jama' (the assessed/expected amount) and 'Hasil' (the amount actually collected). The state tried to maximize cash collections.

fun_activity.title: 🍅 The Time-Traveling Pizza
fun_activity.instructions: Imagine a Mughal emperor ordering a pizza in the 1500s. It would be impossible! Tomatoes and chilies didn't exist in India until the Portuguese brought them from South America. Next time you eat a spicy Indian curry, remember it's a globalized dish!

exam_tips: 📌 Clearly differentiate between Jama (assessed demand) and Hasil (actual collection).
📌 Remember the term 'Jins-i-Kamil' (perfect crops)—these were cash crops like cotton and sugarcane that the Mughal state encouraged because they brought in more tax revenue.
📌 The Panchayat in Mughal villages was led by a headman (Muqaddam or Mandal) who was responsible for maintaining village accounts.
quick_recap: ⭐ The Ain-i Akbari is part of a larger historical work called the Akbar Nama.
⭐ Silver trickled into India from across the globe in exchange for Indian textiles and spices, creating a highly monetized economy.
⭐ Forests were considered 'mawas' (places of refuge) for rebels and a source of valuable elephants for the army.
